title: Who guards the constitution? The Cabinet Secretary, the Crown and the case for clearer rules
label: 16 September 2026 · The Cabinet Secretary and constitutional safeguards
summary: Former Cabinet Secretary Lord Case explains how the top civil servant, the Prime Minister’s senior aide and the King’s senior aide work together informally to protect the UK’s unwritten constitution; he warns this system relies on trust and custom, has real weaknesses (because advisers are appointed and dismissed by the Prime Minister and much is left to chance) and argues Britain should move, gradually and pragmatically, towards clearer written rules or laws for some key points.

speakers.label: Lord Case
speakers.name: Lord Case
speakers.role: Former Cabinet Secretary and Head of the Civil Service, UK Government

chapters.title: Who the Cabinet Secretary is and what they do
chapters.takeaway: The Cabinet Secretary is a senior adviser and a 'tier 2' constitutional guardian who helps guide the Prime Minister, but has no independent legal powers.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Welcome, Lord Case. To start: what does the Cabinet Secretary actually do in constitutional terms? Are they a guardian of the constitution?

turns.speaker: Lord Case
turns.text: Good morning. The Cabinet Secretary is indeed a constitutional guardian but a 'tier 2' one — that means they advise and support the main people who legally hold power: the Prime Minister and the King.

turns.speaker: Lord Case
turns.text: Practically, the Cabinet Secretary advises the Prime Minister on constitutional questions, coordinates senior civil servants and helps make sure the machinery of government works smoothly.

turns.speaker: Lord Beith
turns.text: Do you have to teach Prime Ministers about constitution basics? Are they often unaware?

turns.speaker: Lord Case
turns.text: Yes. Even well-educated Prime Ministers can lack practical knowledge about constitutional rules and precedents; part of the job is to explain those things clearly.

chapters.title: The informal 'golden triangle' and how it works in a crisis
chapters.takeaway: A small group of senior officials — the Cabinet Secretary, the Prime Minister’s main aide and the King’s main aide — share information privately to avoid surprises and to handle emergencies.

turns.speaker: Baroness Laing of Elderslie
turns.text: You mentioned working with predecessors and others. How important is that network in a crisis?

turns.speaker: Lord Case
turns.text: It's vital. The Cabinet Secretary, the Prime Minister's principal private secretary — that's the PM's main aide — and the King's private secretary form what people call the 'golden triangle'.

turns.speaker: Lord Case
turns.text: That phrase simply describes the three main advisers who exchange information regularly to keep the King and PM out of unexpected situations — the 'no surprises' approach.

turns.speaker: Lord Burnett of Maldon
turns.text: How does that work if the government is falling apart? Can it stop a constitutional meltdown?

turns.speaker: Lord Case
turns.text: They can raise their alert level, share the same facts and make sure advice is consistent. But they are advisers, not decision-makers — they can only warn and explain options to the King or PM.

turns.speaker: Lord Burnett of Maldon
turns.text: Can you give a real example?

turns.speaker: Lord Case
turns.text: Yes. At the end of Boris Johnson's term, someone floated calling an election to avoid being forced out. I pulled out the 1950 'Senex' letter and the so-called Lascelles principles — both are older writings about when a monarch might refuse a Prime Minister's request — to show why that was risky.

turns.speaker: Lord Cryer
turns.text: What is the principal private secretary's role day-to-day?

turns.speaker: Lord Case
turns.text: They are the frequent conduit between Government and the Royal Household, talking several times a week about what the PM is thinking so the King isn't blindsided.

chapters.title: Limits of the system and the danger of reliance on personalities
chapters.takeaway: The current system depends on trust, experience and personal relationships, which makes it fragile — especially because advisers serve at the Prime Minister's pleasure.

turns.speaker: Lord Murphy of Torfaen
turns.text: What are the weaknesses? When would a Cabinet Secretary resign?

turns.speaker: Lord Case
turns.text: A big weakness is that the Cabinet Secretary is appointed and can be dismissed by the Prime Minister, so their independence is limited. Resignation is an option if you believe the PM is doing something constitutionally dangerous.

turns.speaker: Lord Murphy of Torfaen
turns.text: Would a resignation always force a fix?

turns.speaker: Lord Case
turns.text: Not necessarily today. Resignations used to cause bigger shocks. Now, turn-over of senior officials can be frequent, so a single resignation might not stop a government action.

turns.speaker: Lord Bellamy
turns.text: Does that mean the monarchy is a weak safeguard too?

turns.speaker: Lord Case
turns.text: Yes — the King is a vital constitutional figure, but in extreme cases the monarchy alone is a relatively weak backstop because it's unelected and constrained by convention.

turns.speaker: Baroness Laing of Elderslie
turns.text: So informal safeguards rely on 'good chaps' — people behaving decently — but that's not reliable today?

turns.speaker: Lord Case
turns.text: Exactly. Historically many guardians came from similar backgrounds and trusted each other. That social cushion is no longer a defensible way to run a modern state.

chapters.title: Codify or keep tradition? Practical steps short of a full written constitution
chapters.takeaway: Lord Case favors moving toward a written constitution in the long run but suggests pragmatic, legal steps now — for example updating the Cabinet Manual and legally fixing who acts if the Prime Minister is incapacitated.

turns.speaker: Lord Burnett of Maldon
turns.text: You said you're moving towards supporting a written constitution. Do you mean a full written charter or small legal changes?

turns.speaker: Lord Case
turns.text: In the long term I lean towards a written constitution, but I'm pragmatic: that won't happen quickly. Shorter-term, I'd put important conventions into law — make some 'pencil lines' into 'ink'.

turns.speaker: Lord Jones of Penybont
turns.text: Are there examples of useful, smaller changes?

turns.speaker: Lord Case
turns.text: Yes. The Cabinet Manual — a public guide to how government should operate — is badly out of date. Updating it and giving some parts legal backing would help.

turns.speaker: Lord Case
turns.text: Another concrete change is legally requiring a Deputy Prime Minister or a clear succession order so there isn't ambiguity if the PM is unavailable. We shouldn't be guessing who takes charge in a crisis.

turns.speaker: Lord Bellamy
turns.text: Would writing rules push powers to the courts?

turns.speaker: Lord Case
turns.text: Potentially. That's one reason people worry about a written constitution. But some legal clarity is better than leaving everything to ad hoc judgment and personality.

chapters.title: Final reflections: realism about reform and the need for more 'inked lines'
chapters.takeaway: Reforming the constitution should be careful and pragmatic: strengthen certain conventions with law, be realistic about how a full written constitution might come about, and avoid enlarging the monarch's powers.

turns.speaker: Baroness Hamwee
turns.text: Is the constitution getting more vulnerable? How worried should we be?

turns.speaker: Lord Case
turns.text: There's been a growing tendency for governments to ignore precedent. That doesn't prove inevitable decline, but it suggests some conventions should be bolstered in law.

turns.speaker: Baroness Hamwee
turns.text: Would moving to a written constitution 'gum up' government business?

turns.speaker: Lord Case
turns.text: It would be hard to do in normal times. Big constitutional changes usually happen after major national breaks. So be cautious: legislate key protections now rather than expect a complete rewrite overnight.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Any closing thoughts?

turns.speaker: Lord Case
turns.text: No more than: be realistic, aim for clearer 'inked' rules on crucial matters like succession in office and modernise the Cabinet Manual — and don't rely on 'good chaps' alone.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Thank you for your candour and time. This committee will reflect on these practical suggestions.

glossary.definition: The most senior UK civil servant who advises the Prime Minister, leads senior officials and helps run Cabinet business and government coordination.
The staff and organization that support the monarch in official duties, managing their schedule, residences and formal communications.
An anonymous 1950 letter signed 'Senex' discussing when a monarch might refuse a Prime Minister, often cited in constitutional debates.
A set of ideas, from a 1950 memo by a royal private secretary, about the limited circumstances in which a monarch might refuse a Prime Minister's request.
An official public guide setting out how the UK government and its ministers are expected to operate, and how constitutional conventions are applied.
Unwritten but accepted rules and practices that govern how the UK constitution operates, followed by tradition rather than law.
The senior aide to the monarch who manages the King's official business, advice, correspondence and liaison with government.
